newsitem.title: SPAIN: Telefonica strong after cable, tariff news.
newsitem.headline: Telefonica strong after cable, tariff news.

text.p: Shares in Spain's Telefonica were higher on Friday, backed by strong demand ahead of next year's placement despite news of it pulling out of a cable deal and a freeze in the urban phone tariff, dealers said.
At 1150 GMT, Telefonica was up 20 pesetas, 0.76 percent, to 2,665, while the Ibex-35 index was up 0.42 percent to 4,452.27.

"We've had the news about Cablevision and on the (urban) tariff freeze. These should be negative for the stock but it just keeps going up. It's pretty bullish and there's no real fundamental reason, there's just a lot of liquidity and demand," said a trader at a European bank.
But others said that the news on the tariff and the cable deal was already discounted, and this was why the share price had not reacted.

Telefonica said today that it and Sogecable, part of the Canal Plus group, would end their Cablevision joint venture. This followed indications from Brussels that the deal was likely to be banned on the grounds that it would create a dominant position on the Spanish market.
Furthermore the government has confirmed that urban phone tariffs are to be frozen until June 1998.
One analyst at Ibersecurities brokerage said the tariff news was already in the share price.

"It's something the firm had taken into account in its forecasts for the next two years...It would have been a suprise if (tariffs) were to fall, as some reports indicated, about the possibility that there would be pressure on the (Development) Ministry to cut charges."
There may be other factors behind the stock's rise, however, the trader said.

"There's strong demand ahead of the privatisation that's allowing (the stock) to pass off bad news. (The brokerage unit of Banco) Santander has been buying, possibly for an institutional investor. We've seen BBV (brokerage) in there a lot - they could be increasing their own stake."
Both BBV and Santander declined to comment on the share price movement, as a matter of policy.
"I've also seen buying from a German bank," the trader said.
This might be on behalf of a German institution who was unable to get as many Deutsche Telecom shares as they would have liked, he said.
The government is to place its remaining 21 percent stake in Telefonica on the stock market in the early part of 1997.
